title: A Bizarre Sequel to One of Tarantino’s Best Movies
text:
Quentin Tarantino’s 2019 movie-industry dramedy, Once Upon a Time in Hollywood , was, as its title suggests, a fairy tale. The film luxuriated in the Tinseltown of the late ’60s, after the golden age of the old studio system had melted away but just before the arrival of gritty “New Hollywood.” It imagined a world where fossils like the fading TV star Rick Dalton (played by Leonardo DiCaprio) could get one last shot at glory rather than vanish into irrelevance. Most magically, in Tarantino’s reimagining, the decade’s dark conclusion doesn’t happen: The Manson family is thwarted before its members can murder the actor Sharon Tate. Tarantino managed to capture these triumphs through a melodramatic lens—which is why it remains one of the writer-director’s best and most mature works.

 He seems to know that too, which may be why he can’t get away from the world he created. Now audiences are being presented with The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth , a sequel of sorts that strips away almost every aforementioned quality. Dalton is gone; instead, we’re spending time with his sidekick and erstwhile stuntman, Cliff Booth (Brad Pitt), who gave the actor a shoulder to cry on and a pair of fists with which to conquer the Manson family in Once Upon a Time in Hollywood . Tarantino, adhering to a bizarre and self-imposed rule that he can direct only one more project before entering retirement, decided to hand off the script to another hugely accomplished filmmaker, David Fincher. Fincher just so happens to have a far less sentimental outlook on life.

 Removing most of what made Once Upon a Time in Hollywood work results in a sequel with a strange and unbalanced—but at times quite compelling—mashup of tones. The follow-up has a far harsher sensibility and, what’s more, barely a plot for more than half the run time; this is simply a violent action thriller focused in large part on the chillest cat in Los Angeles. Dalton was the previous story’s emotional core, whereas Booth was its steady pulse. A tale that’s all Booth ends up feeling cold and ruthless. Fincher has made many great films in the vein of this one, but after almost two and a half hours, I couldn’t tell whether he and Tarantino agreed on just how scary a guy Booth is supposed to be.

 [ Read: Quentin Tarantino’s ultimate statement on movie violence ] 

 Booth resembles a more rough-and-tumble version of the Fonz: He’s a World War II veteran with dozens of confirmed kills to his name, a stuntman who can pull off any daredevil trick, and someone so charismatic that everyone he runs into swears they’ve met him before, whether they have or not. When we reunite with him in 1977 (eight years after his first appearance), Booth has added a few extra lines to his cool-guy résumé. He now bartends at local tiki joints where girls mud-wrestle, and occasionally runs the projection booth at the New Beverly Cinema (owned, in real life, by Tarantino himself). He also drives cars in some obscure form of demolition derby called “Figure 8 racing.” When he’s not doing all of those activities, he seems to work as a freelance “fixer” of sorts, helping Hollywood folks out of extralegal jams for, well, the good of the movies—which Booth loves more than anything.

 Pitt’s face is looking more worn than it did in 2019, and he exudes a slightly grimmer energy. The actor, however, is clearly comfortable revisiting the role that won him an Oscar. He’s also working with a director he’s collaborated with several times before, dating back to 1995’s Seven . Fincher definitely knows his way around an action set piece—when something exciting happens in Cliff Booth , it’s slick. A home-invasion sequence early on has some really shocking flourishes, and a showdown near the end is perfectly paced and choreographed. The budget is big, and the period detail is largely impressive. Even the folks at Netflix, the home-viewing-happy distributor, seem conscious enough of Fincher’s visual mastery to give the film a limited IMAX run.

 But losing Dalton’s pathos, as well as Tarantino’s bittersweet adoration of a bygone age of Hollywood, leaves The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth searching for a larger point. As Booth himself tells Karen Crosby (the reliably fabulous Elizabeth Debicki), a beleaguered talent agent who becomes the object of his affections, “I hate to admit this to someone I’m trying to seduce, but I’m not that deep.” It doesn’t seem like he’s lying. Booth is content to bounce around town doing what he loves, motivated by his affection for an industry he’s only vaguely still a part of. Eventually, he gets sucked into another plotline involving a fading star, the TV hotshot Charlie Peters (a nervy Scott Caan). Yet that quest seems to kick into gear because something exciting has to unfold in order to justify the movie’s existence.

 What would have been more fascinating was if the tension between Tarantino’s script and Fincher’s direction had come to a proper head. Fincher presents Booth’s vigilante justice as efficient and controlled, if not exactly fun. Ultimately, Tarantino’s take on the character is more compelling. No matter the fact that Fincher can put together a shootout with the best of them, he’s still bringing a different auteur’s vision to the screen; whatever his own perspective might be feels utterly drowned out. Cliff Booth is an interesting viewing experience for fans of either director—but one doomed to be a weirdly unsatisfying one from the get-go.
